_what: Swaying Sweetgrass — pitch 02 in the campgrounds. A meadow left alone, with a path into a clearing and a fire pit in the middle of it. Everything that plays on that page is in this file.
_sources: EVERY ID WAS RESOLVED AGAINST YOUTUBE ON 2026-09-21 rather than typed off the link text that arrived — status, playableInEmbed, lengthSeconds, title and ownerChannelName, off one fetch of each watch page. That is the Jungle Room's rule and the reason the two lists below could be told apart at all: the chapter readings arrived looking exactly like the talks, and the channel is the only thing that distinguishes them.
_rights: THE FIRE AND THE READINGS ARE TWO LISTS BECAUSE THEY CARRY TWO RIGHTS STATEMENTS, and this is the decision the room is built around. Ryan's brief pointed at a 21-chapter playlist of Braiding Sweetgrass read aloud. It is uploaded by The Anarchist Audio Library and it is an unauthorised reading of a book that is in copyright — Milkweed Editions, 2013, Robin Wall Kimmerer living and publishing. Every chapter plays and every chapter embeds, so nothing would have stopped it going in as a screen. What stops it is that this room's whole argument is the honorable harvest: never take the first, never take more than you need, ask permission. A page making that argument cannot serve somebody else's whole book off its own surface. So the readings are DOORS and not screens — named, linked, and labelled as what they are — and the borrow link to the real audiobook sits beside them. Ryan's call, 2026-09-21, after the provenance was put to him: both, her voice as the fire and the readings as a door. make-sweetgrass.py refuses a reading marked 'screen', which is how that decision survives somebody tidying it later.
_fire: AUTHORISED RECORDINGS OF KIMMERER IN HER OWN VOICE, which is what the fire pit tells. Her publisher, her university hosts, her conference keynotes, her interviews. Ordered shortest first, so somebody with three minutes and somebody with an hour are both served by the same list without either having to read all of it.
_runtime: EVERY SCREEN AND EVERY DOOR CARRIES ITS RUNTIME, and make-sweetgrass.py refuses one without. Same promise as make-latibulum.py, make-den.py, make-club.py and the Hermitage's campfire: the number is what lets somebody decide before they press. A door needs it as much as a screen does — more, because the press leaves this site.
_teachings: THE FIELD GUIDE, AND IT IS NOT OURS. Six teachings from Indigenous organisations, institutes and nations, Ryan's selection, plus one Kimmerer Q&A he filed with them. Nothing here is summarised or paraphrased on the page: a sweetgrass teaching belongs to the person giving it and the community it is given in, so the room links the video, names the channel, and says what it is about in one line of our own rather than retelling it.
_braid: THE 21-STRAND TEACHING IS TRANSCRIBED FROM ONE OF THE VIDEOS ALREADY IN THE FIELD GUIDE — Sweet Grass Teaching, Shawenim Abinoojii Inc., kb0eGlH8usg — and it was matched to that video rather than guessed at: the transcript panel was opened and read, and the words at 0:53 through 2:54 are the ones on the page. THE VIDEO DOES NOT NAME THE ELDER SPEAKING. The description says only 'Made for Shawenim Abinoojii Inc.', there is no name card at the end, and the channel does not say. So the page credits the organisation and the video and states plainly that the speaker is unnamed there, rather than inventing a name or quietly dropping the question — the herbarium's refusal to guess at a binomial, applied to a person. The words are auto-captions, which are a machine's guess at speech: they are lightly punctuated here and the timestamps are kept so anybody can check them against the video.
_quotes: FOUR PASSAGES FROM BRAIDING SWEETGRASS, all four supplied by Ryan. Three of them are verbatim on our own published pages and were checked against the Knowledge System mirror rather than retyped: the sheaf, the braid of stories and 'becoming indigenous to a place' each appear on glossary/nature, glossary/place-based-education and space/offline. THE FOURTH IS NOT ON ANY PAGE OF OURS and could not be confirmed against the book from here — archive.org's search-inside is unreachable and Google Books rate-limited every attempt on 2026-09-21. It is published on Ryan's word, which is written down here rather than left to look like the others. Star Stuff's zine No. 72 carries a standing caveat on the third one too: a Stimpunks post had attributed it to Barry Lopez, the zine corrected it to Kimmerer, and said it had not yet confirmed it against the book rather than against quotation sites. That caveat is still open and the room says so.
_grass: RYAN'S OWN VIDEO, and it is not sweetgrass — he said so when he sent it. It is already published by us: stimpunks.org embeds this exact guid on the Nature glossary entry, on Play, and on the Offline space page, which is why it belongs in a room built out of those three pages. Ten seconds of a backlit clump of bunchgrass in seed with a mullein rosette at its foot, limestone and river rock, a wall behind. THE SPECIES IS NOT NAMED, for the herbarium's reason: nobody here determined it, and a plant named on a page reads as a determination. VideoPress is the first non-YouTube, non-Spotify frame on this street and its origin had to be added in three places — _headers, love-embed.js and this room's generator.
_borrow: A borrow link is required and a buy link is not — make-hermitage.py's rule, and it matters more here than anywhere: the room is arguing that access to knowledge is mutual aid while sitting next to an unauthorised copy of the book it is arguing from. The Open Library work id was resolved against their search API on 2026-09-21 and the scan it points at answered 200. The WorldCat link is the one our own glossary already cites.

braid.speaker: an Elder, not named on the video
braid.intro: we divide these 21 into seven seven and seven … we divide them into seven strands each and that's what we braid into the one braid

bundles.words: the first seven they always represent those seven generations behind us — our parents, our grandparents, our great grandparents. Who we are, what we are, is because of them, because they're the ones that give us life. At least for that we need to be thankful.
strands: the ones who gave us life

bundles.words: these next seven they represent those seven sacred laws we all talk about … and the old people they tell us those teachings are simple. Love — it's not complicated, nothing complicated about it. Those teachings are powerful. Respect — powerful teaching. They say those teachings are really beautiful. Humility — when I can understand that I'm no better than anybody else, but then nobody else is any better than me.

the last seven, those seven generations ahead of us — our children, our grandchildren, whose children that are yet to be born. Why are they important? What we do to Mother Earth today is one day going to affect them. Right now she gives us everything we need to have life, but if we don't look after it, what's going to be left?

braid.close: so we make that one braid, we bring them and make it into one braid, and in that way each of these strands they also represent yesterday today and tomorrow, man woman and child, mind body and spirit. You could take one strand, break it — that's simple. When you bring them all together, that's what creates that strength of that braid.
braid.roots: our whole journey, our whole life, is intertwined within this braid as well, and it begins right here with the roots that we don't see. Imagine a tree without any roots — a little bit of wind will come, that tree will fall down.

quotes.text: Hold out your hands and let me lay upon them a sheaf of freshly picked sweetgrass, loose and flowing, like newly washed hair. Golden green and glossy above, the stems are banded with purple and white where they meet the ground. Hold the bundle up to your nose. Find the fragrance of honeyed vanilla over the scent of river water and black earth and you understand its scientific name: Hierochloe odorata, meaning the fragrant, holy grass. In our language it is called wiingaashk, the sweet-smelling hair of Mother Earth. Breathe it in and you start to remember things you didn't know you'd forgotten.
quotes.checked: verbatim in the Knowledge System mirror on 2026-09-21

quotes.text: I could hand you a braid of sweetgrass, as thick and shining as the plait that hung down my grandmother's back. But it is not mine to give, nor yours to take. Wiingaashk belongs to herself. So I offer, in its place, a braid of stories meant to heal our relationship with the world. This braid is woven from three strands: indigenous ways of knowing, scientific knowledge, and the story of an Anishinabekwe scientist trying to bring them together in service to what matters most. It is an intertwining of science, spirit, and story — old stories and new ones that can be medicine for our broken relationship with earth, a pharmacopoeia of healing stories that allow us to imagine a different relationship, in which people and land are good medicine for each other.
quotes.checked: verbatim in the Knowledge System mirror on 2026-09-21

quotes.text: Native scholar Greg Cajete has written that in indigenous ways of knowing, we understand a thing only when we understand it with all four aspects of our being: mind, body, emotion, and spirit. I came to understand quite sharply when I began my training as a scientist that science privileges only one, possibly two, of those ways of knowing: mind and body. As a young person wanting to know everything about plants, I did not question this. But it is a whole human being who finds the beautiful path. That September pairing of purple and gold is lived reciprocity; its wisdom is that the beauty of one is illuminated by the radiance of the other. Science and art, matter and spirit, indigenous knowledge and Western science — can they be goldenrod and asters for each other? When I am in their presence, their beauty asks me for reciprocity, to be the complementary color, to make something beautiful in response.
quotes.checked: NOT on any page of ours, and not confirmed against the book from here — see _quotes. Published on Ryan's word.

quotes.text: It was through her actions of reciprocity, the give and take with the land, that the original immigrant became indigenous. For all of us, becoming indigenous to a place means living as if your children's future mattered, to take care of the land as if our lives, both material and spiritual, depended on it.
